claims.text: The starting material is additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy.
The starting alloy has an fcc matrix.
Elevated-temperature degradation in oxidizing or reducing gases is governed by selective oxidation of Cr and Ti.
Selective oxidation of Cr and Ti produces oxide phases at grain boundaries.
The Cr- and Ti-rich grain-boundary oxides are brittle.
Cr and Ti are more reactive than the relevant competing alloy constituents under oxidizing conditions.
Cr- and Ti-rich oxides accumulate at grain boundaries.
Accumulation of brittle grain-boundary oxides disrupts cohesive strength and initiates microstructural degradation of the fcc matrix.
Oxidizing exposure at 800–1000°C will cause grain-boundary embrittlement.
Oxidizing exposure at 800–1000°C will reduce mechanical integrity through formation of Cr- and Ti-rich oxides.
Reducing exposure will produce less degradation than oxidizing exposure.
Reducing exposure will produce minimal oxide formation and retain mechanical properties.
Before exposure, the alloy has notable strength and fatigue performance.
The proposed mechanism applies between 800°C and 1000°C.
Gas environments with sufficient chemical potential can drive selective oxidation or reduction reactions in this alloy.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis broadly states that degradation during either oxidizing or reducing exposure is governed by selective oxidation, but the mechanism is limited to oxidizing conditions and the prediction for reducing conditions is minimal oxidation and retained properties. No distinct degradation pathway is supplied for reducing gases.
